# Colony History
[italic]A short history of Solaris Gulch for new arrivals, as the Herald's archive tells it. Most arrivals are only passing through.[/italic]
## A Long Way Out LV-747 was catalogued by the Kepler surveys back in 2026 and then left alone for a very long time. It sits at the far end of the Neroid Sector, too remote for anyone to settle while there were closer worlds to take. In the end its surface rights went cheap to a private company that thought it had found a shortcut.
## The Lichen Gamble - The shortcut was [bold]lichen[/bold]. Instead of an atmosphere processor, the owners seeded the gulch with hardy imported strains, sold to their investors as the cheap way to make a world breathe. Nobody had ever proven it worked. - The first two imported batches took hold. The batches grown in the colony's own labs, [bold]Eta[/bold] and [bold]Lambda[/bold], never thrived. - The dust storms kept coming, and every storm added to the repair bill. By 2144 the money was gone.
## The Quiet Sale In 2145 the colonial director sold Solaris Gulch to [bold]Weyland-Yutani[/bold] without telling the people who lived here. Most of them found out when the lab doors were rekeyed and their old passes stopped working. The lichen labs were stripped and turned into storage and study units for biological samples. A few lichen techs copied the sale notice onto the backs of old lab forms, wrote under it in plain words what it meant for every contract in the colony, and pinned the sheets up in the canteen. Nobody else would learn about their own sale from a locked door. Those sheets were the first Herald.
## Big Red Today - Around 120 people remain, and every one of them works for the Company, willingly or not. - On paper the colony is a biological storage depot and virology lab. Talk in the canteen says even that work has stopped. The Company pays for upkeep and nothing more. - Its star is a dying orange giant, far brighter than Sol. The storms still roll in off the flats, and every building keeps its shutters for a reason.
Off-worlders call it a dead end. The Herald keeps the archive anyway, so that nobody forgets this was meant to be a living world.
